commands.desc: Initialize an empty bare repository
commands.tooltip: A bare repository holds only Git's internal data with no working tree, so no files are ever checked out. Bare repos are the standard layout for central shared remotes and self-hosted servers. Push into one directly and clone from it like any other remote.

commands.desc: Clone a full mirror of a repository
commands.tooltip: A mirror clone is a bare copy that includes every branch, tag, and remote ref exactly as on the origin. Use it to back up a repository or migrate it to another host. Keep it in sync later with git push --mirror.

commands.desc: Clone a repository and all its submodules
commands.tooltip: A submodule is a nested Git repository pinned to a specific commit inside another repository. The --recurse-submodules flag initializes and checks out every submodule right after the clone finishes. Without it the submodule directories stay empty until you run git submodule update --init.

commands.desc: Clone history only since a given date
commands.tooltip: A shallow clone downloads only commits newer than the given date, cutting transfer size for very old histories. The commit graph is truncated, so operations like git log --follow or merging deep history may need to fetch more. Use --depth 1 for the absolute minimum history.

commands.desc: Clone a repository without file contents
commands.tooltip: A partial clone, here blobless, fetches commits and trees but defers file versions until you actually need them. Files download on demand when you check out or diff them, making huge repositories clone fast. It is a good fit for monorepos and very large codebases.

commands.desc: Clone only a single branch of a repository
commands.tooltip: The --single-branch flag fetches just the named branch instead of every branch and tag. Pair it with --branch to pin the checkout to a specific branch or tag, like a release line. It is handy for CI jobs and for exploring one version without downloading everything.

commands.desc: Show compact status with branch and tracking info
commands.tooltip: Adding --branch to the short format puts the current branch and its upstream on the first line, like main...origin/main [ahead 2]. The remaining lines use two-column shorthand, XY, for staging and working-tree state. It is the compact status most people use day to day.

commands.desc: Print status in a stable script-friendly format
commands.tooltip: The porcelain format is a guaranteed-stable variant of the short format designed for scripts and tools to parse. Its output never changes between Git versions, unlike human-oriented output. Use it in CI checks instead of parsing git status -s.

commands.desc: List ignored files alongside normal status
commands.tooltip: Shows tracked, untracked, and ignored files in one view, with ignored paths under their own section. It is useful for spotting .gitignore patterns that no longer match anything. Combine it with --short for a compact listing.

commands.desc: Summarize changed files with line counts
commands.tooltip: Prints one line per changed file with insertions and deletions drawn as plus and minus bars, plus a final total. It answers what changed and how much without any patch detail. Append it to most diff commands, such as git diff --stat origin/main.

commands.desc: Show numeric add and delete counts per file
commands.tooltip: The numstat format is a machine-friendly diff summary with tab-separated added, deleted, and filename columns. Scripts use it to compute churn or estimate review size. Binary files show a dash in both count columns.

commands.desc: List only the names of changed files
commands.tooltip: Prints just the file paths touched between the two commits, with no diff content. It is the fastest way to get the file list for a commit, a range, or your working tree. Pipe the output to tools like xargs to lint only the changed files.

commands.desc: Show changes word by word instead of line by line
commands.tooltip: A line-based diff hides small edits inside a long line, so --word-diff splits changes at word boundaries instead. Deleted words appear wrapped in [- -] and added words in {+ +}. It shines for prose, config files, and long JSON lines.

commands.desc: Flag whitespace errors in a diff
commands.tooltip: Scans the diff for trailing whitespace, space-before-tab, and blank-line-at-EOF problems and lists each occurrence. It is a common pre-commit gate in CI pipelines. The command returns a non-zero exit code when errors are found, so scripts can fail the build.

commands.desc: Show the latest changes to a single file
commands.tooltip: Diffs the named path between the previous commit and the working tree, filtering the patch to just that file. The HEAD~1 syntax means the commit one step before HEAD. Use HEAD~3 or a branch name to look further back.

commands.desc: Diff two files outside a repository
commands.tooltip: The --no-index mode compares two arbitrary files or directories with the normal diff engine, even outside any Git repository. It reports differences with the same patch formatting Git always uses. Useful for spotting drift between two config files or generated outputs.

commands.desc: Mark a new file as intent-to-add
commands.tooltip: The -N flag registers a new file so git diff and git diff --stat start showing its content before it is staged. The file appears in the index as empty rather than untracked. Follow up with git add when you are ready to stage the real content.

commands.desc: Edit the staged patch in your editor
commands.tooltip: Stages the file but opens the generated patch in your editor first, letting you hand-edit hunks before they enter the index. It is a surgical alternative to git add -p when you know exactly what belongs in the commit. Save and close the editor to apply the edited patch.

commands.desc: Preview what git add would stage
commands.tooltip: Reports which files would be added, modified, or removed without changing the index. Run it before a big git add to confirm the staging set. Add -v to see per-file verdicts in more detail.

commands.desc: Set the executable bit while staging
commands.tooltip: Stages the file and marks it executable in one step, avoiding a second commit just for the file mode. The opposite form --chmod=-x clears the executable bit. Handy for scripts added on Windows, where the bit is often wrong.

commands.desc: Commit with a different author identity
commands.tooltip: Overrides the author recorded in the new commit, useful for committing on behalf of someone else or fixing a misconfigured identity. The value is a display name plus an email in angle brackets. Git still records you as the committer.

commands.desc: Mark a commit to squash into the previous one
commands.tooltip: Creates a commit tagged as a squash target for the named commit, usually the one just before it. During an interactive rebase, git rebase -i folds squashed commits into their target. Unlike --fixup, the squash marker keeps your message so you can edit the combined one.

commands.desc: Commit with a backdated timestamp
commands.tooltip: Sets the author date of the commit instead of using the current clock. Common for keeping imported history in order or correcting an inaccurate system clock. Git accepts most date formats, including ISO dates and relative forms like 3 days ago.

commands.desc: Commit without running hooks
commands.tooltip: Bypasses the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks for this one commit, so checks like linters and spellers do not run. Use it sparingly for emergency fixes; the -n shorthand does the same. It does not affect push hooks, which need --no-verify on git push instead.

commands.desc: Show the diff while writing the commit message
commands.tooltip: Opens the editor with the staged diff appended below the message template, so you can review exactly what you are about to commit. The diff is stripped from the final message automatically. It is a great habit for writing accurate commit messages.

commands.desc: Commit using a message read from a file
commands.tooltip: Reads the commit message from the named file instead of the editor or -m. Useful for changelog-driven workflows and for long or script-generated messages. Trailing whitespace and comment lines are cleaned according to your cleanup mode.

commands.desc: Fix the author of the last commit
commands.tooltip: Rewrites the most recent commit with a corrected author line, leaving the message untouched. Useful after spotting a wrong identity or email in the last commit. Amending changes the commit hash, so avoid it once the commit has been pushed.

commands.desc: Show the last ten commits, one line each
commands.tooltip: Combines the compact one-line format with a count limit, giving the ten most recent commits as abbreviated hash and subject. The -10 is shorthand for -n 10. It is the fastest way to orient yourself in a branch.

commands.desc: Visualize all branches as an ASCII graph
commands.tooltip: Draws the commit history as a graph with branch topology, decorating each commit with its branch and tag names. The --all flag includes every ref, not just the current branch. It is the classic command behind the popular lg alias.

commands.desc: Find commits that changed a string count
commands.tooltip: The pickaxe -S option lists commits where the number of occurrences of the given string changed. It catches additions, removals, and renames of a function or constant. Add --pickaxe-regex to treat the argument as a regular expression.

commands.desc: Find commits whose diff matches a regex
commands.tooltip: The -G option lists commits whose patch adds or removes a line matching the regular expression. Unlike -S it matches line content rather than count changes, so it finds every touched line. Quote the pattern so the shell does not interpret it.

commands.desc: List commits by a specific author
commands.tooltip: Filters the log to commits whose author matches the given pattern, matched as a substring against name and email. Combine it with --since for a time window or --grep for message text. Use --committer to filter by who committed instead.

commands.desc: Track a file's history across renames
commands.tooltip: Walks the history of the named file and follows it through renames, so the log reaches back before the file changed name. Without --follow the history stops at the rename point. The double dash tells Git everything after it is a path, not a revision.

commands.desc: Show commit summaries with file stats
commands.tooltip: Prints each commit followed by a diffstat of the files it touched, like a compact per-commit report. It gives the shape of a change without the full patch. Add -p to include the actual diff.

commands.desc: List only merge commits
commands.tooltip: Filters the log to merge commits, which have two or more parents. Handy for finding where branches were integrated or spotting accidental merges. Flip it with --no-merges to see only ordinary commits.

commands.desc: List commits excluding merges
commands.tooltip: Shows only non-merge commits, useful for reviewing the actual work in a branch without the merge noise. It pairs well with --first-parent to trace the mainline. Many teams use it for changelog generation.

commands.desc: Follow only the mainline of history
commands.tooltip: Walks the first parent of every commit, so merged branches appear as single commits instead of expanding into their full history. It shows what actually happened on the branch itself. Ideal for reviewing a long-lived feature branch.

commands.desc: Print the log with a custom format
commands.tooltip: Replaces the default log layout with placeholders: %h for short hash, %an for author name, and %s for subject, among many others like %ad for date. It is the building block for custom log aliases and scripts. Quote the format string so the shell does not expand it.

commands.desc: List commits before a given date
commands.tooltip: Limits the log to commits older than the given date, the mirror of --since. Combine both to window a specific period, like --since='2024-01-01' --until='2024-03-01'. Any date Git understands works, including relative forms like 3 months ago.

commands.desc: List commits that modified files
commands.tooltip: Filters commits by the type of change in their diff: M for modified, A for added, D for deleted, R for renamed, and C for copied. A commit shows up when any of its files match. Chain letters like --diff-filter=AM to match several kinds.

commands.desc: Show the evolution of a line range
commands.tooltip: Traces every change to lines 40 through 60 of the named file, printing each commit that touched them with its patch. The range follows the lines as they move within the file. It is line-level archaeology, far more precise than file-level git log.

commands.desc: Show the latest commit in detail
commands.tooltip: Prints the most recent commit with its metadata, message, and full patch. It is the natural entry point when you want to see what just happened. Add --stat for a summary or pass a branch name like git show origin/main.

commands.desc: Show a file as of an older commit
commands.tooltip: Prints the content of the named path at the given revision without touching your working tree. The revision:path syntax works for any commit, tag, or branch. Use it to inspect an old version before deciding to check it out.

commands.desc: Summarize the latest commit's changes
commands.tooltip: Shows the newest commit with a file-by-file diffstat instead of the full patch. Add --name-only to get just the file list. It is a quick way to judge the size and shape of the last change.

commands.desc: Print the raw content of a Git object
commands.tooltip: cat-file is the low-level tool for reading Git objects: -p pretty-prints, -t prints the type, and -s prints the size. Running it on HEAD shows the commit object with its tree, parents, and message. It is the plumbing behind many higher-level commands.

commands.desc: Resolve a ref to its full commit hash
commands.tooltip: Resolves a name like HEAD, a branch, or a tag into the full 40-character object hash. Scripts use it to capture commit IDs reliably. Add --short for the abbreviated form and --abbrev-ref for branch names.

commands.desc: Print the current branch name
commands.tooltip: Resolves HEAD to the short branch name, like main, instead of the raw hash. On a detached HEAD it prints HEAD instead of a branch. It is the script-friendly way to ask which branch you are on.

commands.desc: Print the short hash of the current commit
commands.tooltip: Resolves HEAD to the abbreviated hash Git uses in log output, typically seven characters. Useful for build tags and cache keys in scripts. The length follows core.abbrev or disambiguation rules.

commands.desc: Count the commits reachable from HEAD
commands.tooltip: Counts every commit reachable from the given ref, which is the total history length of the branch. Add a range like main..feature to count only commits unique to feature. CI scripts use it for versioning and change detection.

commands.desc: Show last-touched info with short dates
commands.tooltip: Blame annotates each line with the commit and author that last changed it; --date short trims timestamps to YYYY-MM-DD for easier scanning. Useful on large files where full timestamps create noise. Combine it with -L 10,20 to limit the line range.

commands.desc: Blame while ignoring whitespace changes
commands.tooltip: The -w flag ignores whitespace-only edits, so blame attributes lines to the commit that last changed their content. It stops a reformat commit from claiming authorship of every line. Combine it with -M to follow lines moved within the file.

commands.desc: Summarize commits per author with emails
commands.tooltip: shortlog groups commits by author and sorts by count; -s keeps just the number, -n sorts numerically, and -e appends each author's email. It is the standard contributor leaderboard. Add a range like v1.0..HEAD to scope it to a release.

commands.desc: Search tracked files for a pattern
commands.tooltip: Greps the current checkout without touching untracked files, which plain grep cannot distinguish. It is faster than scanning the whole tree because only tracked files are searched. Use -i for case-insensitive matches and -n for line numbers.

commands.desc: Search only files matching a path pattern
commands.tooltip: Restricts the search to paths matching the pattern after the double dash, here JavaScript files only. The -n flag adds line numbers. The pathspec is a glob, so '*.js' hits files in any directory.

commands.desc: List files that contain a match
commands.tooltip: Prints only the filenames that contain the pattern, with no match lines, perfect for feeding into scripts. The -l flag stands for files-with-matches. Pass a revision like v1.0.0 to search a specific commit instead of the working tree.

commands.desc: Stash changes but keep the staged ones
commands.tooltip: Stashes the working-tree changes while leaving the index, the staged set, intact so you can test exactly what is staged. The -k shorthand does the same. Use it when staging one fix but wanting to set aside the rest.

commands.desc: Stash including untracked files
commands.tooltip: By default stash ignores untracked files, so -u, or --include-untracked, sweeps them in too. The -m flag names the stash for easier identification in git stash list. Use -a to also stash ignored files, though that is rarely needed.

commands.desc: Show the diff inside a stash
commands.tooltip: Displays the changes held by the named stash as a patch. Without -p it prints a short stat instead. stash@{0} is the most recent stash, stash@{1} the one before it, and so on.

commands.desc: Apply the latest stash without removing it
commands.tooltip: Restores the most recent stash, stash@{0}, into your working tree but keeps the stash in the list, unlike git stash pop which drops it. Apply is the safe choice when you might want the stash again. Give a stash id to apply an older one.

commands.desc: List branches with tracking and ahead-behind info
commands.tooltip: The doubled -v adds each branch's upstream and how many commits it is ahead of or behind that upstream. It answers whether your local branch has unpushed work at a glance. Compare with git status --short --branch for a single-branch view.

commands.desc: List branches fully merged into HEAD
commands.tooltip: Shows branches whose commits are all reachable from the current branch, meaning their work is already integrated. These are the safe candidates for deletion with git branch -d. Pass a ref like --merged origin/main to check against the remote instead.

commands.desc: List branches with unmerged commits
commands.tooltip: Lists branches that contain commits not reachable from the current branch, so their work is still outstanding. Deleting one of these needs -D instead of -d and throws those commits away. Review this list before any cleanup session.

commands.desc: Print the current branch name
commands.tooltip: Prints the name of the checked-out branch and nothing else, with no decoration. Unlike git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD it exits non-zero on a detached HEAD. Scripts prefer it when they need a clean branch name.

commands.desc: List branches matching a name pattern
commands.tooltip: Shows only branches whose names match the glob pattern, here every branch under the feature/ namespace. It is the filtering form of git branch. Combine it with -r for remote-tracking branches like 'origin/*'.

commands.desc: Set the tracking remote for a branch
commands.tooltip: Configures the local main branch to track origin/main, so pull, push, and status know the upstream. The -u shorthand is equivalent. Do this once after creating a local branch that mirrors a remote one.

commands.desc: List branches that contain a commit
commands.tooltip: Shows every branch that includes the given commit or tag in its history. It is the reverse lookup to git tag --contains. Useful for checking which branches already picked up a fix.

commands.desc: List branches by last commit date
commands.tooltip: Sorts branches by committer date, newest first when the key is negated. The bare --sort=committerdate puts oldest first. It is a quick way to spot stale branches that deserve review or deletion.

commands.desc: Delete a remote-tracking branch locally
commands.tooltip: Removes the local copy of a remote branch, origin/feature-x, without touching the remote itself. It cleans up stale tracking refs, which git fetch --prune also does automatically. The -r flag targets remote-tracking branches only.

commands.desc: Switch back to the previous branch
commands.tooltip: Checks out the branch you were on before, like cd - for directories. It reads the previous branch from the reflog, so it works across several switches. Great for toggling between two branches during review.

commands.desc: Check out a tag with a detached HEAD
commands.tooltip: Checks out the given commit or tag without creating a branch, leaving HEAD detached. Any commits made here belong to no branch and can be lost, so create a branch first if you plan to work. Use it to inspect or build an old release.

commands.desc: Create a branch with no shared history
commands.tooltip: Creates a new branch that shares no commits with the current one, as if history started fresh. The index and working tree stay as they are. It is the standard trick for gh-pages and other content-only branches.

commands.desc: Restore a file from an older commit
commands.tooltip: Replaces the working-tree copy of the file with its content from the given revision. The --source flag selects where the content comes from; without it restore uses the index. It is the modern replacement for the git checkout commit file form.

commands.desc: Restore a file in index and working tree
commands.tooltip: Resets the file in the index, unstaging it, and in the working tree, discarding local edits, in one move. It returns the file to its state in the last commit. Be careful: local changes to that file are lost.

commands.desc: Unstage everything
commands.tooltip: Moves every staged change back to the working tree, leaving files modified but unstaged. It is the modern equivalent of git reset HEAD with a dot pathspec and does not touch file contents. Run it before re-staging with a finer-grained git add.

commands.desc: Discard all uncommitted changes
commands.tooltip: Replaces every tracked file in the working tree with its staged version, throwing away all local edits. There is no undo for this, so check git status and git diff first. Untracked files survive; remove those with git clean.

commands.desc: Create a local branch tracking a remote one
commands.tooltip: Creates a local branch named after origin/feature-notifications and sets it to track that remote branch in one step. The -t flag stands for --track. It is the fastest way to start working on a branch that exists only on the remote.

commands.desc: Apply selected hunks from a file
commands.tooltip: Walks through the file's diff hunk by hunk, asking whether to apply each one to the working tree. It is the reverse of git add -p: selecting what to discard or check out. Answer y, n, or s to split a hunk and control the result.

commands.desc: Merge only if it can fast-forward
commands.tooltip: Merges the remote branch only when the merge is a pure fast-forward with no divergence, and aborts with an error otherwise. The flag makes the merge safe and predictable for scripted updates. If it fails, decide between a real merge or a rebase.

commands.desc: Finish a merge after resolving conflicts
commands.tooltip: Completes a conflicted merge once you have fixed the files and staged them, reusing the prepared merge message. It is the merge counterpart of git rebase --continue. Resolve all conflicts and git add the files before running it.

commands.desc: Merge without creating a commit
commands.tooltip: Performs the merge and stages the result but leaves the final commit for you to make or inspect. Useful for reviewing the combined tree before committing. A later plain git commit finishes the merge.

commands.desc: Skip the current commit during a rebase
commands.tooltip: Tells a conflicted rebase to drop the commit being applied and move on to the next one. Use it when the commit is no longer wanted, not when it just needs conflict fixes. Fix conflicts and run git rebase --continue instead, or --abort to bail out entirely.

commands.desc: Rebase with local changes stashed automatically
commands.tooltip: Stashes uncommitted changes before rebasing and pops them back afterwards, so a dirty working tree no longer blocks the operation. Without it Git refuses to rebase with local modifications. The stash is reapplied on top of the rebased branch.

commands.desc: Unstage a single file
commands.tooltip: Removes the named file from the index, turning it back into a modified or untracked file while keeping its content. It is the classic unstage command, now superseded by git restore --staged. Nothing in the working tree changes.

commands.desc: Remove a file from the repo and disk
commands.tooltip: Deletes the named file from the working tree and stages the removal in one step. The deletion lands in your next commit. Use --cached to keep the file on disk while untracking it, and -r for directories.

commands.desc: Untrack a file but keep it on disk
commands.tooltip: Stops tracking the file while leaving it in the working tree, so it becomes untracked. It is the right move for secrets or build artifacts you want to keep locally but stop committing. Add the file to .gitignore right after, or it will show as untracked forever.

commands.desc: Remove an entire directory recursively
commands.tooltip: Deletes the directory and everything inside it from both the repo and disk, staging all the removals. The -r flag is required for directories. Double-check the path, because the files are gone from the working tree after this.

commands.desc: Rename a file and stage the change
commands.tooltip: Moves or renames a tracked file in one step, staging both the deletion and the addition. Git detects it as a rename in diffs. For moving into a subdirectory, the target directory must already exist.

commands.desc: Remove only ignored files and directories
commands.tooltip: Deletes ignored files and directories from the working tree: -f forces, -d includes directories, and -X targets only ignored paths. Use it to purge build artifacts while keeping your own files. Run git clean -n first to preview exactly what would be removed.

commands.desc: List tags matching a name pattern
commands.tooltip: Shows tags whose names match the glob, here every tag starting with v1. Add --sort=-creatordate to order them newest first. It is the quick way to enumerate release lines.

commands.desc: Force a tag to point at another commit
commands.tooltip: Moves an existing tag to a new commit, overriding the error a plain git tag would raise. Tags pushed to a shared remote are a contract, so only do this for unpublished or broken tags. If the tag is already pushed, the remote needs a force update.

commands.desc: Push a single tag to the remote
commands.tooltip: Pushes just the named tag instead of every tag. Use it to publish one release without flooding the remote. The remote stores it under refs/tags/v1.0.0.

commands.desc: Delete a tag on the remote
commands.tooltip: The empty source before the colon tells the remote to delete refs/tags/v1.0.0, removing the tag there but not locally. Use it to unpublish a wrong release tag. Delete the local tag afterwards with git tag -d.

commands.desc: Set your global Git name
commands.tooltip: Writes the name attached to all your commits into ~/.gitconfig, so every repository on this machine uses it unless overridden locally. Git records this name in every commit you make. It is one half of the identity setup, along with user.email.

commands.desc: Set your global Git email
commands.tooltip: Writes the email used in commit authorship into ~/.gitconfig. Many hosting services attribute commits by this email, so it should match the one on your account. Check the current value with git config --global user.email.

commands.desc: Default new repositories to main
commands.tooltip: Sets the branch name that git init creates, replacing the historical master default. New repositories start on main instead of needing a rename later. It does not change existing repositories.

commands.desc: Create a shortcut for a Git command
commands.tooltip: Defines co as an alias for checkout, so git co works like git checkout. Aliases live in ~/.gitconfig under the alias section and accept arguments and flags. For complex commands, quote the whole string.

commands.desc: Create a pretty-log alias
commands.tooltip: Adds an lg alias that prints a decorated graph of all branches, one commit per line. It is the most imitated Git alias in the wild. Run git lg after defining it.

commands.desc: Set VS Code as the commit editor
commands.tooltip: Tells Git to open Visual Studio Code for commit messages and rebase todo lists. The --wait flag is required because Git needs the editor process to block until you finish. Other editors work too, like vim or nano.

commands.desc: Show all effective Git settings
commands.tooltip: Prints every configuration value in effect, merged from system, global, and repository scope, later files winning. Add --show-origin to see which file each value came from. Use it to debug mysterious Git behavior.

commands.desc: Read a single config value
commands.tooltip: Prints the value of the named key, here the URL of the origin remote. It exits non-zero if the key is unset, which scripts can detect. The general form works for any setting name.

commands.desc: Save credentials to a plaintext file
commands.tooltip: Caches your username and password in ~/.git-credentials in plain text, so future pushes and pulls skip the prompt. Anyone with access to your home directory can read those credentials. Prefer a helper like cache, libsecret, or an SSH key instead.

commands.desc: Convert CRLF line endings on commit
commands.tooltip: For Linux and macOS, the input setting converts CRLF endings to LF when committing while leaving the working tree alone. It keeps repositories consistent for teams mixing Windows and Unix. Windows users usually set true instead.

commands.desc: Enable colored output in terminals
commands.tooltip: Turns on color for Git output when writing to a terminal, and off when piping to a file or another program. The auto mode keeps scripts free of escape codes. It is a long-standing default in modern Git but can be set explicitly.

commands.desc: Make git pull rebase by default
commands.tooltip: Changes git pull to rebase local commits onto the fetched branch instead of creating merge commits. The result is a linear history without merge noise. It matches the workflow of teams that always pull with --rebase.

commands.desc: Add an upstream remote for a fork
commands.tooltip: Registers a second remote named upstream pointing at the original repository you forked. Fetching from it keeps your fork in sync with the source project. The convention is origin for your fork and upstream for the canonical repo.

commands.desc: Rename a remote
commands.tooltip: Changes the name of the remote from origin to upstream and updates every tracking branch and config that references it. Use it when restructuring remote layouts. Existing refs like origin/main move to upstream/main.

commands.desc: Inspect a remote in detail
commands.tooltip: Prints the remote's URLs plus which local branches track which remote branches, and whether pushes would fast-forward. It contacts the remote by default, so it can be slow on flaky networks. Add -n to skip the network call.

commands.desc: Delete stale remote-tracking branches
commands.tooltip: Removes local refs like origin/dead-branch whose remote counterparts no longer exist. It is the manual form of git fetch --prune. Run it when git branch -r shows branches you know were deleted upstream.

commands.desc: Print a remote's URL
commands.tooltip: Shows the URL Git uses for the named remote, useful for confirming https versus SSH endpoints. Add --push to see the push URL when it differs. Scripts use it to detect the hosting platform.

commands.desc: Fetch a single branch from a remote
commands.tooltip: Downloads the named branch's commits and updates its remote-tracking ref without merging anything. It is the surgical version of git fetch. The branch lands in origin/feature-branch, ready to inspect or merge.

commands.desc: Fetch all tags from the remote
commands.tooltip: Downloads every tag the remote has that you lack, in addition to the usual branch updates. Tags are not fetched by default unless they point at fetched commits. Use it after a release to pull in new version tags.

commands.desc: Pull and rebase local commits on top
commands.tooltip: Fetches origin/main and replays your local commits on top of it instead of merging, giving a linear history. It is the explicit form of a rebase pull for a specific remote and branch. Set pull.rebase true to make it the default.

commands.desc: Pull only when it fast-forwards cleanly
commands.tooltip: Updates the branch only if the local branch can fast-forward to the remote, and aborts otherwise. A failure means your local commits diverge from the remote, so a merge or rebase is needed. It prevents surprise merge commits in automated pulls.

commands.desc: Pull with local changes stashed first
commands.tooltip: Stashes uncommitted working-tree changes before pulling and restores them afterwards. Without it a dirty tree can block the pull. Conflicts between the stash and the new commits need manual resolution.

commands.desc: Preview a push without sending it
commands.tooltip: Shows exactly which commits and refs would be pushed, then stops without transferring anything. Use it to sanity-check what an unpushed branch contains. The -n shorthand does the same.

commands.desc: Push commits and their annotated tags
commands.tooltip: Pushes the branch and any annotated tags pointing at commits in the pushed range. Lightweight tags are not included. It keeps release tags in sync with the code that introduced them.

commands.desc: Push every local branch
commands.tooltip: Pushes all local branches to the named remote, not just the current one. New branches appear on the remote automatically. It never deletes remote branches; use --prune for that.

commands.desc: Show the pinned commit of each submodule
commands.tooltip: Lists every submodule with the commit it is pinned to, plus a prefix: a space for up to date, a dash for not initialized, and a plus for a different commit than recorded. It is the first stop when submodule content looks wrong.

commands.desc: Unregister a submodule from the repo
commands.tooltip: Removes the submodule's entry from the configuration and clears its working tree, so it no longer appears in git submodule status. The -f flag is needed when the submodule has local changes. The gitlink entry in the index stays until you commit.

commands.desc: Export the repo as a zip with a prefix
commands.tooltip: Bundles the current commit's tree into a zip file without any .git history. The --prefix option nests everything under myapp/ so unzipping into a directory does not scatter files. Use it for source drops and releases.

commands.desc: Show the size of the object database
commands.tooltip: Reports how many loose objects and packs exist and how much disk the repository uses. The -H flag prints sizes in human-readable units like MiB. Run it before and after git gc to see the cleanup effect.

commands.desc: Run housekeeping only when needed
commands.tooltip: Runs garbage collection only if Git estimates the repository needs it, based on loose object and pack counts. Git calls it automatically after many operations. Run the full git gc manually when you want a forced cleanup.

commands.desc: Run scheduled repository maintenance
commands.tooltip: Executes the maintenance tasks Git considers due, which on modern Git replaces most manual gc invocations. The --auto form is what Git triggers after fetch and commit operations. Configure recurring runs with git maintenance start.

commands.desc: Check the entire object database
commands.tooltip: Verifies every object's integrity, connectivity, and format, reporting dangling or corrupt objects. The --full flag scans all packs and loose objects. Run it after crashes or disk issues to assess repository health.

commands.desc: Test whether a path is ignored
commands.tooltip: Prints the path if .gitignore rules ignore it and exits zero, or exits non-zero if the file would be tracked. Scripts use it to verify ignore patterns. Add -v to see which specific rule matched.

commands.desc: List every file in a commit
commands.tooltip: Lists the full file tree of HEAD recursively, one path per line, without touching the working tree. The -r flag recurses into directories and --name-only suppresses hashes and modes. It answers what files a commit contains, not just the checkout.

commands.desc: Get the nearest tag name only
commands.tooltip: Prints the most recent tag reachable from HEAD without the commit-count and hash suffix git describe normally appends. CI scripts use it as a clean version number. Fall back to --always for repositories with no tags.

commands.desc: Print the installed Git version
commands.tooltip: Shows the Git version plus platform details, like git version 2.43.0. Scripts parse it to gate features that need newer Git. The short form git -v prints the same output.

commands.desc: List all local branch refs
commands.tooltip: Prints every local branch as a full hash plus refs/heads/name pair. It is the plumbing-level view of what git branch shows. Add --tags to include tags, or no flag to list every ref in the repository.

commands.desc: Open a diff in an external tool
commands.tooltip: Launches your configured diff tool, like meld, vimdiff, or VS Code, for the given range instead of printing a text patch. Configure the tool with git config diff.tool. It is best for large or visual review sessions.

commands.desc: Open a merge tool for conflict resolution
commands.tooltip: Starts your configured merge tool on each file with unresolved conflicts, one after another. Configure the tool with git config merge.tool. After resolving a file it asks whether the resolution is correct before moving on.
